title: Good surprises and worry secrets
keyIdea: A good surprise is a happy secret, like a present or a party, and everyone finds out soon. A worry secret makes you feel scared, sad or sick, or someone says you must never tell. Warning signs are words like “It’s our special secret”, “You will be in trouble” or “Nobody will believe you”, and sweets or presents to keep quiet. Always tell a trusted grown-up about a worry secret, even if you promised not to. You will not be in trouble for telling.
familyTip: Use the word surprise for happy things at home: “This is a surprise for Gran. We will tell her on Saturday.” Then say plainly: “In our family we don’t keep secrets, only surprises. If anyone ever asks you to keep a secret that worries you, tell me or your teacher, even if you promised.” Ask your child to name three grown-ups they would tell.

visual.caption: Good surprise or worry secret? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A present for Dad on Friday
A party for Gran on Saturday
A cake for Mum on Sunday

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort surprises from worry secrets, find the day each is told, spot worry feelings and warning words, and help Mia tell.

kid: A good surprise is a happy secret. You hide a present or plan a party. Soon everyone finds out, and they smile.
A worry secret is not like that. It makes you feel scared, sad or sick inside. Or someone says you must never tell. Ask: will everyone find out soon? Does it feel happy? If not, it is a worry secret.
Some words are a warning. “It’s our special secret.” “You will be in trouble if you tell.” “Nobody will believe you.” Sweets or a toy to keep quiet are a warning too.
Tell a worry secret to a grown-up you trust, like Mum, Dad, Gran or your teacher. Tell even if you promised. You will not be in trouble. If they are busy, tell someone else.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. The PSHE Association Programme of Study for key stage 1 asks children to learn the difference between good surprises and secrets that should be shared, to recognise when something feels unsafe, and how to ask a trusted adult for help. The DfE Relationships Education guidance (2019) includes knowing when it is right to break a confidence and how to report a concern. The NSPCC PANTS rule “Speak up, someone can help” and its advice to talk about surprises rather than secrets are the model here.

Two simple tests do most of the work at this age. Time: a surprise has an end, a day when everyone finds out. Feeling: a surprise feels exciting; a worry secret feels scary, sad, confusing or sick. Children are also told to notice what the other person says. Safeguarding guidance lists “special secret”, threats (“you’ll get in trouble”, “I’ll hurt you”), “nobody will believe you” and gifts for silence as common grooming and bullying tactics.

Common mistakes: thinking a secret called special or fun must be a good one; thinking a present makes it all right; believing a promise must always be kept; telling only a toy, a friend or the person who asked for the secret; and stopping after one busy adult. Some children also mix up excited butterflies with real worry, so naming body feelings helps.

Use the word surprise at home for happy things, and say you don’t keep secrets in your family. Practise who they would tell and what they would say: “I have a worry secret.” In the lab your child sorts cards, puts each secret on the day it is told, taps worry feelings and warning words, and helps Mia tell a trusted grown-up even though she promised.

practice.prompt: You and Dad hide a present for Mum. You will give it to her on Sunday. What is it?
choices: A secret to keep for ever
practice.hint: Will Mum find out soon? Will she be happy?
practice.explain: It is a good surprise. Mum finds out on Sunday, and it makes her happy.

practice.prompt: You keep a surprise for {n} days. Then you wait {k} more days, and everyone finds out. How many days is that?
practice.hint: Start at {n} and count on {k} more days.
practice.explain: {n} days and {k} more make {=n+k} days. A surprise has an end: then everyone finds out.

practice.prompt: Someone says, “If you tell, you will be in trouble.” What is that?
choices: A warning sign: tell a grown-up
practice.hint: Would a happy surprise need a scary rule like that?
practice.explain: It is a warning sign. Tell a trusted grown-up. You will not be in trouble for telling.

practice.prompt: You name {n} grown-ups you trust at home and {k} at school. How many grown-ups can you tell?
practice.hint: Count the grown-ups at home, then count on the ones at school.
practice.explain: {n} and {k} more make {=n+k} trusted grown-ups. If one is busy, you can tell another.

practice.prompt: A secret makes your tummy feel sick. What does that tell you?
practice.hint: Do happy surprises make you feel sick?
practice.explain: A sick, scared or sad feeling means it is a worry secret. Tell a trusted grown-up.

pool.prompt: A grown-up says, “Don’t tell your mum. It’s our special secret.” What do you do?
pool.hint: Should a grown-up ask you to hide things from Mum?
pool.explain: Tell. Calling it special does not make it good. A grown-up should not ask you to keep secrets from Mum.

pool.prompt: Someone gives you sweets and says, “Keep quiet.” Is it a good secret now?
choices: No, it is a worry secret
Yes, if I like the sweets
pool.hint: Why would someone pay you to keep quiet?
pool.explain: No. Sweets or presents to keep quiet are a warning sign. Tell a trusted grown-up.

pool.prompt: You promised to keep a secret. Now it makes you scared. Can you tell?
choices: No, a promise is a promise
Only if they say I can
pool.hint: Which matters more: the promise or being safe?
pool.explain: Yes. You can break a promise to keep a worry secret. Telling is the right thing to do.

pool.prompt: Who should you tell about a worry secret?
choices: The one who told me to keep it
pool.hint: Who can do something to help you?
pool.explain: Tell a trusted grown-up, like your teacher or Mum. A teddy cannot help, and the person who asked will not.

pool.prompt: Your class plans a party for your teacher on Friday. What is it?
choices: A secret to keep for ever
pool.hint: Does it have a day when everyone finds out?
pool.explain: A good surprise. Your teacher finds out on Friday, and it makes them happy.

pool.prompt: It is Monday. Gran’s party is in {n} days. Then she will know. How many days until Gran finds out?
pool.hint: The party day is when Gran finds out.
pool.explain: {n} days. A surprise has a day when everyone finds out.

pool.prompt: You tell your teacher a worry secret, but she is busy. What next?
pool.hint: Keep going until a grown-up listens.
pool.explain: Tell another trusted grown-up, like Mum, Dad or Gran. Keep telling until someone listens.

pool.prompt: Which one is a warning sign?
pool.hint: Which words try to stop you telling?
pool.explain: “Nobody will believe you” tries to stop you telling. It is a warning sign. Grown-ups will listen.

pool.prompt: {n} friends plan a surprise for Dad. {k} more friends join in. How many friends are in on the surprise?
pool.explain: {n} friends and {k} more make {=n+k} friends. Dad will find out on his birthday.

pool.prompt: Will you be in trouble for telling a worry secret?
choices: Yes, I will be told off
pool.hint: What do trusted grown-ups want you to do?
pool.explain: No. You will not be in trouble for telling. Trusted grown-ups want to know so they can help.
